R1000.description: The pull_request_target trigger runs the workflow with the target repository's permissions even when the code comes from an external fork, which can expose secrets to unreviewed code.
R1000.suggestion: Replace pull_request_target with pull_request, or if it's required, make sure not to check out the PR's code and explicitly restrict permissions.
R1001.description: The workflow is triggered by pull_request_target (a privileged context with access to secrets) and this checkout step explicitly sets ref: {ref}, pulling in the PR's code (potentially from an untrusted fork) to run it with those privileges.
R1001.rule: Checkout of the PR head in a pull_request_target context
R1001.suggestion: Avoid checking out the PR head in a workflow triggered by pull_request_target. If unavoidable, don't execute the PR's code (limit yourself to reading metadata), or split the logic into a second, minimally-privileged workflow that consumes artifacts instead of executing code directly.
R1002.description: The action {uses} uses a mutable tag instead of a commit hash. The tag can be reassigned to a different commit at any time without the workflow file changing.
R1002.suggestion: Replace the tag with the exact commit hash of the version you want to use. Example: {action}@<full-40-character-hash>.
R1003.description: The job "{job_name}" has no permissions block defined at either the workflow or job level. GITHUB_TOKEN inherits the repository's default permissions, which can be excessively broad.
R1003.suggestion: Add an explicit permissions block with the minimum permissions required. Example: permissions: contents: read
R1004_AUDIT.description: harden-runner is configured in audit mode, meaning it logs outbound calls but doesn't block them. The pipeline can talk to any external server without restriction.
R1004_AUDIT.suggestion: Change egress-policy from audit to block and define an allowlist of permitted domains with allowed-endpoints.
R1004_MISSING.description: The job "{job_name}" doesn't have step-security/harden-runner configured. Without it, there is no mechanism monitoring or filtering the pipeline's outbound network traffic.
R1004_MISSING.suggestion: Add step-security/harden-runner as the job's first step with egress-policy: block and an allowlist of permitted domains.
R1005.description: An outbound call to the domain {domain} was detected in a run command. This domain is flagged as suspicious and is commonly used in data exfiltration attacks.
R1005.rule: Outbound call to a suspicious domain
R1005.suggestion: Remove the call to this domain. If it's required for the pipeline to work, review its purpose and make sure it's justified and documented.
R1006.description: The job "{job_name}" uses a self-hosted runner. Unlike GitHub-hosted runners, self-hosted runners persist state across runs and may have access to the internal network, widening the blast radius if the pipeline is compromised.
R1006.suggestion: Consider using GitHub-hosted runners instead of self-hosted. If self-hosted is required, make sure the runner is properly isolated and configure harden-runner to limit outbound network traffic.
R1007.description: The action {uses} belongs to the "{org}" organization, which is not in the list of trusted verified organizations. If this action is compromised, it could run malicious code in the pipeline with access to all its secrets.
R1007.suggestion: Verify that the action {uses} is trustworthy, review its source code, and replace the tag with a pinned commit hash. Consider whether this action is actually necessary or can be replaced with an official alternative.
R1008.description: The action {uses} has no action.yml or action.yaml file in its repository, which means it isn't properly published to the GitHub Marketplace.
R1008.rule: Action not found in the Marketplace
R1008.suggestion: Verify that the action {uses} exists and is properly published. Consider replacing it with an official Marketplace alternative.
R1009.description: An outbound call to the IP address {ip} was detected in a run command. Using raw IPs is an evasion technique that bypasses domain-name-based network filtering.
R1009.rule: Outbound call to a raw IP address
R1009.suggestion: Remove the call to this IP. If it's required for the pipeline to work, review its purpose and consider using a domain name instead so it can be properly filtered by harden-runner.
R1010.description: The job "{job_name}" publishes an artifact with no integrity verification mechanism. An artifact tampered with during the build could reach production undetected.
R1010.suggestion: Add a digital signing step with cosign after publishing the artifact to guarantee its integrity. Example: uses: sigstore/cosign-installer followed by cosign sign <image>.
R1011.description: The third-party action {uses} has access to GITHUB_TOKEN. If this action is compromised, it could use the token to interact with the GitHub API with all its permissions, publish malicious releases, or modify the repository.
R1011.rule: Third-party action with access to GITHUB_TOKEN
R1011.suggestion: Verify that the action {uses} is absolutely necessary and trustworthy. Restrict GITHUB_TOKEN's permissions to the minimum required via the permissions block, and consider using a reduced-scope token instead of GITHUB_TOKEN.
R1012.description: The action {uses} uses "{version}" as its version, which looks like a branch name rather than a tag or commit hash. A branch updates with every commit, meaning the workflow can run different code on every run with no control over it.
R1012.rule: A branch is used as the action version
R1012.suggestion: Replace the reference to branch "{version}" with a pinned commit hash or a stable version tag. Example: {action}@<40-character-hash>.
R1013.description: The workflow is triggered by any pull request against any branch of the repository, with no restriction at all. This unnecessarily widens the attack surface.
R1013.suggestion: Add a branch restriction to the pull_request trigger. Example: on: pull_request: branches: [main]
R1014.description: The step's "{key}" field has a value hardcoded directly in the file instead of using a GitHub Actions secret. Anyone with access to the repository can see this credential.
R1014.suggestion: Replace the hardcoded value with a reference to a GitHub Actions secret. Example: {key}: ${{{{ secrets.SECRET_NAME }}}}
R1015.description: A DNS query was detected with an unusually long subdomain ({length} characters). This technique is used to exfiltrate data by encoding it into DNS subdomains, evading HTTP-based network filters.
R1015.suggestion: Remove the use of dig or nslookup with unusually long subdomains. If DNS queries are required in the pipeline, document their purpose and make sure they don't contain encoded sensitive data.
R1016.description: The run command directly expands the expression "${{{{ {expression} }}}}" inside a bash script. An attacker who controls that expression's value can inject arbitrary commands that will run with the pipeline's permissions.
R1016.rule: Expression injection in a run command
R1016.suggestion: Assign the expression's value to a step environment variable and reference it from bash instead. Example: env: VALUE: ${{{{ {expression} }}}} and then use $VALUE in the run command instead of the expression directly.
R1017.description: The action {uses} uses "@latest" as its version. This is the most unstable reference possible, since it always points at the latest commit on the action repository's main branch. Any change the author pushes runs automatically on the next workflow run with no control at all.
R1017.rule: Use of @latest on a third-party action
R1017.suggestion: Replace @latest with a pinned commit hash that guarantees the exact same code always runs. Example: {action}@<40-character-hash>.
R1018.description: A call to the GitHub API was detected pointing at the hardcoded repository "{repo}". This technique can be used to exfiltrate data to an attacker-controlled external repository, taking advantage of api.github.com being a trusted domain.
R1018.rule: Possible exfiltration via the GitHub API
R1018.suggestion: Verify that the GitHub API call is legitimate and necessary. If the target should be the repository itself, use ${{{{ github.repository }}}} instead of a hardcoded value.
R1019.description: The variable "{variable}" holds a value derived from a secret and is being printed in the pipeline logs. GitHub doesn't mask variables derived from secrets, so the value will appear as plain text in the logs.
R1019.suggestion: Remove any command that prints variables derived from secrets. If debugging is needed, use add-mask to mask the value: echo "::add-mask::${variable}"
R1020.description: The job "{job_name}" runs on a self-hosted runner with labels suggesting a cloud instance ({cloud_labels}). Without hardening configured, any process in the pipeline can query the instance metadata service to obtain the associated IAM role's credentials and access the entire cloud infrastructure.
R1020.rule: Self-hosted runner on a cloud instance without hardening
R1020.suggestion: Configure harden-runner with egress-policy: block to limit outbound network traffic. Make sure the instance's associated IAM role has minimal permissions, and consider blocking access to the metadata service from the pipeline.
R1021.description: The workflow uses pull_request_target as a trigger and checks out the PR by number with gh pr checkout. This creates a time window between PR approval and checkout during which an attacker can push malicious code. The workflow will run the new code instead of the approved one.
R1021.suggestion: Replace gh pr checkout with actions/checkout using ref: ${{{{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}}} to pin the exact approved commit hash. This guarantees the code that was reviewed is always what runs.
R1022_JOB.description: The "if" condition of job "{job_name}" combines extra text with a ${{{{ ... }}}} expression, or chains several expressions together. GitHub Actions evaluates "if" as true whenever the final result is a non-empty string, so the expression's real boolean result is ignored and the job always runs.
R1022_JOB.rule: if condition always evaluates to true
R1022_JOB.suggestion: Write the condition as a single expression that fills the whole field: if: ${{{{ <expression> }}}}, with no extra text before or after it and no concatenated expressions.
R1022_STEP.description: The "if" condition of a step in job "{job_name}" combines extra text with a ${{{{ ... }}}} expression, or chains several expressions together. GitHub Actions evaluates "if" as true whenever the final result is a non-empty string, so the expression's real boolean result is ignored and the step always runs.
R1022_STEP.rule: if condition always evaluates to true
R1022_STEP.suggestion: Write the condition as a single expression that fills the whole field: if: ${{{{ <expression> }}}}, with no extra text before or after it and no concatenated expressions.
R1023.description: The action {uses} uses a major version whose runtime (Node.js 12/16) is no longer supported by current GitHub Actions runners. This can cause the step to fail, degrade in functionality, or be silently skipped by GitHub.
R1023.rule: Action with an outdated runtime incompatible with current runners
R1023.suggestion: Update {action} to a recent major version compatible with Node 20/24, checking the action's changelog to adapt to any API changes between major versions.
R1024.description: The job "{job_name}" uses "{label}" in runs-on, which doesn't match any recognized GitHub-hosted runner label or self-hosted preset. It may be an outdated or misspelled label, or a retired image, causing the job to fail or queue indefinitely.
R1024.suggestion: Verify that the label matches a current GitHub-hosted runner image in the official documentation, or explicitly include the "self-hosted" label if this is your own runner.
R1025.description: The action {uses} corresponds to a version affected by {vuln_id}: {summary}
R1025.suggestion: Update {action} to a later version not affected by {vuln_id} ({reference}) and pin it to a commit hash.
ui.about_p1: Zenith Engine is a static security analysis tool for GitHub Actions workflows. Upload your .yml or .yaml file and get an immediate analysis of the security vulnerabilities present, classified according to the OWASP CI/CD Security Risks TOP 10.
ui.about_p2: For each vulnerability detected, the exact line where it occurs, its severity level, and a concrete suggestion for fixing it are shown.
ui.no_vulnerabilities: ✅ No vulnerabilities detected in this workflow.
ui.parse_error: Couldn't parse the file as a valid GitHub Actions workflow. Make sure it's a single YAML document (no multiple '---'-separated blocks) and that its top level is a mapping of keys like 'on', 'jobs', etc.
